prompt: I teach grade 6 science. Make me an interactive figure for tomorrow's lesson on why summer is hotter than winter. I've got about 10 minutes before my next class.
summary: I've built your seasons figure for grade 6. A sunbeam 1 m wide hits the ground at noon in a place 40° north (about as far north as Madrid, New York or Beijing). A date slider runs from 21 January to 21 December and a switch turns Earth's tilt on and off. As the date moves to winter, the sun sinks and the beam spreads along a ruler on the ground. On 21 June it covers 1.04 m and on 21 December 2.24 m. A 24-hour bar shows daylight shrinking from 15 hours to 9. A meter shows the day's total sunlight dropping to 30% of June's. A small graph shows how high the noon sun is in each month. The readout does the sum on screen, e.g. "100 ÷ 2.24 = 45% of the strength of a sun straight overhead". With the tilt switched off, every day has 12 hours of light and the same 50° noon sun, so there are no seasons. The caption also corrects the common belief that distance causes seasons: Earth is closest to the sun in January. Under the figure, a note says what it leaves out: seasons are swapped south of the equator, air and clouds absorb some sunlight, and the hottest weeks come about a month after the longest day. The challenge is to find the month with the widest beam and the shortest day (21 December). I checked it at the start and end of the slider, with the tilt off, in dark mode and at phone width. On a phone, the ruler and graph labels come out small.
